fields.title: RDC – Tshopo : présence opérationnelle des partenaires dans la réponse à la MVE-BVD au 31 août 2026
fields.body:
Au 31 août 2026, neuf organisations appuyaient le ministère de la Santé publique, dans le cadre du Système de gestion de l’incident (SGI), pour la préparation et la réponse à la 17ᵉ épidémie de maladie à virus Ebola dans la province de la Tshopo.

La présence opérationnelle comprend deux agences des Nations Unies, trois ONG internationales, une ONG nationale, deux organisations intergouvernementales et un observateur. Les interventions sont principalement concentrées dans les zones de santé affectées, notamment Tshopo, Kabondo, Mangobo, Lubunga, Wanierukula et Bafwasende. Plusieurs zones de santé à risque demeurent toutefois insuffisamment couvertes.

Les partenaires soutiennent les principales fonctions de la réponse : coordination, surveillance épidémiologique, recherche active des cas et suivi des contacts, prise en charge, prévention et contrôle des infections, vaccination, services de laboratoire et logistique. Les interventions couvrent également la communication sur les risques et l’engagement communautaire, la gestion des données, la formation, ainsi que la santé mentale et le soutien psychosocial.

Cette cartographie présente la répartition géographique et les domaines d’intervention des partenaires. Elle contribue à identifier les lacunes de couverture, à renforcer la coordination opérationnelle et à orienter la mobilisation des ressources vers les zones affectées et à risque prioritaires.

**Source :** Cluster Santé – 3W, août 2026.

fields.title: Présence opérationnelle des partenaires nationale MVE-BVD au 31 août 2026
fields.body:
Au 31 août 2026, le Cluster Santé en République démocratique du Congo (RDC) recensait 94 acteurs humanitaires ayant communiqué leur présence opérationnelle à travers le 3W (Who does What, Where? – Qui fait Quoi, Où ?) et contribuant à la mise en œuvre du plan SGI du Ministère de la Santé pour la réponse à la maladie à virus Ebola.

La présence des partenaires se compose de 43 ONG internationales, 40 ONG nationales, 6 agences des Nations Unies, 3 institutions gouvernementales et 2 observateurs.

Les partenaires appuient plusieurs fonctions essentielles de la réponse, notamment : la coordination, la surveillance épidémiologique et la recherche des contacts, la prise en charge des cas, la prévention et le contrôle des infections (PCI), la vaccination, les services de laboratoire, la communication sur les risques et l’engagement communautaire, l’eau, l’hygiène et l’assainissement (WASH), la logistique, la formation, la gestion des données et de l’information, ainsi que la santé mentale et le soutien psychosocial.

La présence opérationnelle est principalement concentrée dans les provinces affectées par Ebola, notamment l’Ituri, le Nord-Kivu, le Sud-Kivu, le Haut-Uélé, le Bas-Uélé et la Tshopo, avec des niveaux de couverture variables selon les provinces.

Cette cartographie fournit une vue d’ensemble de la répartition géographique et de l’empreinte opérationnelle des partenaires de santé. Elle facilite l’identification des lacunes de couverture et des zones prioritaires, et constitue un outil essentiel de coordination et de planification pour orienter la priorisation des ressources, renforcer la couverture opérationnelle et appuyer une prise de décision fondée sur les données dans le cadre de la réponse nationale à Ebola.

Source : Cluster Santé – 3W, août 2026.

fields.title: As confirmed deaths from Ebola reaches more than 3,000 in Democratic Republic of Congo, Concern further ramps up its response
fields.body:
The Irish humanitarian organisation has adapted its current programming to include Ebola prevention and preparedness activities to try and limit the spread of the virus. More than 70,000 people have been reached through Ebola awareness activities, with information on how to protect themselves from the virus.

32 health workers have been trained in areas such as infection prevention and control standards and protocols, hand hygiene in healthcare settings, and waste management. 10 handwashing stations have been completed, with Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) kits provided to four health facilities to protect healthcare staff and patients from the spread of the disease, while in two health facilities minor rehabilitation of water infrastructure is ongoing.

“It is three months since the World Health Organisation announced DRC’s 17th Ebola outbreak, with this one on course to be the deadliest yet. For the Congolese people this is one crisis on top of many others, not least being forced from their homes due to conflict. Neither the outbreak, nor the conflict, show any signs of slowing, both exacerbating basic yet essential needs,” said David Jones, Concern’s country director in DRC.

“Distrust in the healthcare system and a reluctance to seek treatment for suspected Ebola cases is impacting its containment. Working with communities, communicating clearly and honestly with them, listening to them and local leaders is essential in this response, as is ensuring people have the practical resources to protect themselves from the outbreak. Access to water, basic sanitation through toilets, and hygiene kits including soap and buckets are just three of the ways Concern is offering support. Concern has strong relationships with the communities it serves, from years of working in the areas now affected, and we are exceptionally well placed to respond effectively as a result.”

The virus is ‘growing exponentially’ according to the World Health Organisation, in the north and east of the country, and the spread of infections now covers an area larger than France. Six provinces are impacted, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo and Bas Uélé. North Kivu alone has the same population as Ireland.

Transmission rates are higher than the rate observed during the Ebola outbreaks in West Africa in 2014 to 2016, and previously in DRC from 2018 to 2020. The fatality rate among confirmed cases is 48.6% as of 30th August.

In zones that have not had any Ebola cases, prevention and protection is essential. In Kirotshe, 15 kilometres from the frontline of active conflict, Concern are providing public handwashing stations, hygiene and sanitation kits as well as rehabilitating water sources. That’s alongside cash distributions to people forced from their homes due to fighting, so they can meet their basic needs, including feeding their families and replacing essentials they had to leave behind when fleeing their homes.

Concern has been working in DRC since 1994. Part of its work has been to address the country’s decades-long humanitarian crisis, particularly in the east, through providing support for livelihoods, nutrition, gender equality, and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH).

To support Concern’s Ebola Emergency Appeal, click [here](https://www.concern.net/donate/ebola-emergency-social-appeal/inline-checkout).

***For further information contact Eilis Staunton, Media Relations Officer, Concern Worldwide, at eilis.staunton@concern.net or +353 85 872 0720.***

fields.title: On the frontlines of infection prevention for Ebola control
fields.body:
**Mongbwalu, Democratic Republic of the Congo—**In the stifling heat of Mongbwalu General Reference Hospital in Ituri Province, the epicentre of the ongoing Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, the clatter of disinfection buckets echoes through the corridors. The scent of chlorine lingers in the air as health workers dash from ward to ward.

Amid the bustle, Nadège Esangowale Yangala walks with quiet determination. An Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) specialist, she is on the frontlines of the Ebola response, working as a consultant with the World Health Organization (WHO).

“When I leave a health facility knowing the staff are better protected and able to work safely, I know our collective efforts are saving lives,” says Yangala, who has worked in public health for 13 years.

Since the outbreak was declared in mid-May 2026, Yangala has been part of the frontline response, helping health facilities strengthen infection prevention and control. Her mission is vital: protect health workers and patients while reinforcing community trust.

“IPC and WASH are the first line of defence against Ebola,” she says. “Without strict measures, hospitals can become places where the virus spreads.”

When Ebola strikes, health facilities become high-risk environments. Every consultation, every patient and every procedure carries potential exposure. Proper use of personal protective equipment (PPE), strict hand hygiene and rigorous patient triage are essential. Yangala works to ensure these practices become routine because they are key to preventing transmission and stopping the virus from spreading.

Every day, she assesses infection prevention measures and works with health teams to strengthen them. She helps ensure clear separation between clean and contaminated areas, improve hand hygiene and triage stations at facility entrances, and ensure patients move safely through designated care pathways.

She recalls a visit to Mongbwalu General Reference Hospital where she found the triage desk located inside a crowded waiting room. Within 48 hours, working with the local team and partners including WHO, Médecins Sans Frontières, Action Against Hunger and UNICEF, the space was completely reorganized. Mandatory triage was moved to the entrance, foot-operated handwashing stations were installed and a temporary isolation area was created.

Days later, a person suspected of having Ebola was identified and safely isolated on arrival, preventing exposure to other patients and unprotected staff.

But Yangala’s work extends far beyond infrastructure. Much of her time is devoted to training and mentoring health workers in early detection, immediate isolation, the safe donning and removal of protective equipment, medical waste management and decontamination.

She does more than teach. She observes, corrects and encourages. “Every training session and every protocol properly applied is one less chain of transmission,” she says.

With WHO’s support, Yangala leads practical field training, distributes IPC supplies, helps improve access to safe water and strengthens the safe management of medical waste.

In just two months, 13 health facilities in Mongbwalu Health Zone were brought up to IPC standards, while around 430 personnel—including healthcare workers, traditional healers, IPC-WASH supervisors, decontamination teams and safe burial teams—received training and on-site mentorship.

Challenges remain significant. Interruptions in the supply of water, soap, chlorine and protective equipment, staff fatigue and resistance to change continue to test the response. Yet Yangala remains convinced that every action matters.

Over the months, she has witnessed a remarkable shift. Hand hygiene and equipment disinfection have become routine. Patient flows are now clearly organized in almost all supported facilities. Health workers increasingly see IPC not as an added burden, but as essential protection for themselves and their families.

She remembers one nurse who initially dismissed the new practices as too demanding. A few weeks later, she watched him train his colleagues with discipline and conviction. “These simple actions save lives,” he would tell them.

For Yangala, that transformation is as much a human victory as it is a professional one. The impact of her work—and that of her colleagues—is reflected in the renewed confidence of health workers, the solidarity among teams and the reassurance of people seeking care.

Behind every handwashing station installed, every training delivered and every supervisory visit lies a single purpose: making health facilities safer and saving lives.

Yangala’s work demonstrates the vital role of infection prevention and control in the Ebola response. She helps ensure that health workers can provide care safely, patients can seek treatment with confidence, and communities continue to trust their health facilities.

fields.title: PAMOJA-DRC: four years of commitment to strengthening citizen participation and local governance in the DRC
fields.body:
On 27 June 2026, the PAMOJA-DRC consortium, led by Acted and co-funded by the European Union, marked the conclusion of nearly four years of work with an event held simultaneously in Kinshasa and in the six provinces covered by the project: Ituri, Tshopo, North Kivu, South Kivu, Maniema and Tanganyika.

Implemented against a backdrop of security crises, population displacement, overexploitation of natural resources and persistent mistrust between citizens and institutions, the programme aimed to strengthen civic dialogue and community participation in local decision-making processes. In many of the programme’s areas of operation, civil society organisations (CSOs) and community radio stations play a vital role in voicing the concerns of local people, but face constraints in terms of institutional, organisational and technical capacity. PAMOJA-DRC was therefore developed to strengthen these local actors so that they can better represent the needs of communities, promote accountability among the authorities and contribute to more inclusive and sustainable development.

Screening of a documentary as part of activities to raise awareness and promote public dialogue.

During the project, 24 Congolese civil society organisations and 12 community radio stations received comprehensive support aimed at strengthening their institutional, organisational, technical and digital capacities. In particular, CSOs were supported through the Grassroots Organisation Capacity Assessment (GOCA), a diagnostic and capacity-building tool developed by Acted and used for over a decade with civil society organisations in various contexts. Based on a participatory approach, GOCA assesses the organisational and institutional capacities of organisations across five key dimensions: governance and administration, organisational management, financial management, project cycle management, and external relations and resource mobilisation. This methodology not only helps to identify each organisation’s strengths and needs, but also enables the design of tailored support and the measurement of progress made throughout the project.

In addition, CSOs received training on internal governance, organisational and financial management, advocacy, social auditing, women’s and young people’s rights, and the sustainable management of natural resources. They also received personalised support, peer-to-peer exchanges, IT and communications equipment, and a micro-project funding scheme enabling them to put the skills they had acquired into practice on the ground.

Visitors and participants chat at an exhibition.

Partner radio stations, for their part, were supported in their role as catalysts for public dialogue and in their digital transition. Through training, editorial and technical guidance, and practical support, they have developed new media and audiovisual content that gives greater visibility to the concerns, aspirations and initiatives of local communities. The project also fostered synergies between CSOs, radio stations, public authorities and citizens, notably through public debates, provincial round-table discussions, workshops for sharing experiences and the production of participatory content.

Over the four years of implementation, the supported organisations have carried out numerous initiatives addressing locally identified priorities. In particular, the funded micro-projects have contributed to promoting the rights of indigenous peoples, preventing gender-based violence, reducing land disputes, empowering women economically, protecting the environment and strengthening social cohesion. In Tshopo, for example, several initiatives have helped to strengthen mediation in land disputes and support women’s entrepreneurship in the cassava sector. In Tanganyika, initiatives to prevent gender-based violence have raised awareness within communities whilst supporting the economic empowerment of women’s groups.

Participants, partners and members of civil society gathered for an event focusing on civic expression and the sharing of local experiences.

The results observed demonstrate the gradual strengthening of the organisations supported. The final evaluations carried out in 2026, based on GOCA criteria, show that several CSOs have reached the organisational development stage known as ‘autonomous’, corresponding to the highest level of institutional maturity defined by the tool, whilst others have progressed to the ‘mature’ or ‘well-developed’ stages ’. These results reflect concrete progress in terms of internal governance, administrative and financial management, strategic planning, resource mobilisation and capacity for action. They also confirm the relevance of a methodology combining participatory assessment, training, mentoring, peer exchanges and long-term support to underpin the sustainable development of civil society actors.

The closing event showcased these achievements through audiovisual screenings, debates, theatre performances and artistic performances organised in Kinshasa, Goma, Walungu, Bunia, Isangi, Kindu and Kalemie. In particular, participants were able to view several audiovisual productions created as part of the project, which gave a voice to communities and showcased initiatives led locally by partner organisations and radio stations. In Kinshasa, the documentary \*Petites histoires du Congo profond\* (Short Stories from the Heart of the Congo), directed by filmmaker Dieudonné Hamadi and based on testimonies gathered as part of the programme, illustrated the richness of the experiences and journeys of local stakeholders.

Beyond this celebration, PAMOJA-DRC leaves behind a network of local stakeholders who are better equipped to inform, mobilise and support citizens in the life of their communities. By strengthening the capacities of civil society organisations and community media, the programme has helped to consolidate sustainable spaces for dialogue, citizen participation and accountability within Congolese communities, whilst fostering the emergence of local solutions to the development challenges faced in the east of the DRC.

*Discover all the project’s audiovisual productions on the [PAMOJA platform](https://pamoja.live/productions-pamoja/).*

fields.title: UK accelerates support for efforts to stop Ebola outbreak at source
fields.body:
## Thousands of vulnerable people will be supported by a new package of UK funding

- UK steps up support for affected communities and frontline workers with £50 million package
- Accelerated support comes as outbreak risks becoming deadliest on record
- Africa Minister Kirsty McNeill announced measures on Parliament’s first day back

Thousands of vulnerable people will be supported by a new package of UK funding designed to help tackle the growing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

FCDO Minister for Africa, Kirsty McNeill, has today announced more than £50 million to support efforts to contain the disease, save lives and reduce the risk of further international spread – taking the full UK contribution to £78 million.

This comes as the largest Ebola outbreak in the DRC’s history continues to spread, on course to become the deadliest and most extensive Ebola epidemic ever recorded. This spread is against a backdrop of conflict, displacement and severe humanitarian need, compounding the risk of catastrophe on an unprecedented scale, increasing the urgency of international action.

The new UK package will help strengthen disease surveillance, support frontline health workers, improve infection prevention and control, expand access to treatment, strengthen community engagement and support safe and dignified burials.

On her first appearance at the Despatch Box after Parliament returned, Minister for Africa Kirsty McNeill announced these measures, demonstrating the importance the UK Government attaches to tackling the outbreak.

Minister for Africa Kirsty McNeill said:

> Families across the DRC are living through unimaginable loss as Ebola tears through communities, claiming lives, and leaving thousands more fighting for survival.
> 
> We know that speed saves lives, which is why we were amongst the first to commit support and experts to the region, but as the outbreak intensifies, we are accelerating our response to match the pace and scale of the challenge.

The UK is already supporting the regional response through partnerships with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), the World Health Organization, the United Nations and humanitarian organisations working on the front line. British public health experts have also been deployed across the region to support surveillance, infection prevention, community engagement and outbreak preparedness.

### **Notes to Editors**

- The £51m package announced today consists of:
    - £40m from humanitarian crisis and contingency funding and unallocated spend
    - £11m in re-allocation from existing FCDO allocations

fields.title: Mr. Tom Fletcher, Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator – Virtual Briefing to Member States on the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 1 September 2026
fields.body:
*As delivered*

Excellencies, Distinguished Representatives,

Thank you, Dr. Tedros \[Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO)\], and thank you for hosting us today and for your leadership alongside the fantastic WHO team. It is also great to welcome Ambassador \[Paul Empole Losoko\] Efambe \[Permanent Representative\] of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) \[to the United Nations Office at Geneva\] and so many colleagues from across the IASC \[Inter-Agency Standing Committee\].

Thank you all for joining us.

I also want, before underlining a couple of points on Ebola, to highlight that we will be issuing at the end of the week a Flash Appeal on Nepal, and, as you know, colleagues across the humanitarian family are responding right now to that crisis.

You’ve heard, colleagues, the \[Secretary-General\] sounding the alarm on the Ebola outbreak. You’ve heard Dr. Tedros and I on it repeatedly in recent weeks.

We need to turn that alarm into action.

As Tedros has said, this is the fastest-growing epidemic on record, hitting a country already in a profound humanitarian crisis. Nearly 11 million people already needing support. And with conflict uprooting families, acute food insecurity, and malnutrition at vast levels.

The response is growing, has been scaled up, but the virus is, as you’ve heard, moving faster. And unless we scale up urgently, more lives will be lost and the threat will grow.

The outbreak is now spread across six provinces, including areas where insecurity is limiting our access and where health systems are already weak.

This makes it harder to detect cases, trace contacts, treat patients, and to build trust.

Women and girls, as we’ll hear more of shortly, especially pregnant women, are disproportionately affected.

Children are losing parents and caregivers, making them even more vulnerable to exploitation and trafficking.

So, it is not simply a health emergency. It is also a humanitarian emergency layered onto many existing humanitarian emergencies.

Excellencies,

I commend the Government of the DRC for its leadership, with strong support from WHO, Africa CDC, and through the partnership with the IASC members, and others represented here today.

We activated on June 9, we have strengthened the response.

Damien Mama, the Humanitarian Coordinator, and Julien Harneis, the Senior Ebola Coordinator, will give you a sense of what it looks like on the front lines.

Operational hubs in Bunia and Beni are up and running. Humanitarian financing has been mobilized. And with empowered leadership of Damien, our Humanitarian Coordinator, we have committed, of course, in the context of the Humanitarian Reset, to ensure that we have that single coordinated response behind the \[Humanitarian Coordinator’s\] leadership.

But we cannot respond incrementally to an epidemic, which is now growing exponentially.

So, we need a sustained, large-scale operation that gets ahead of the virus. Expanded treatment capacity. More safe and dignified burial teams. Better access for humanitarian workers and supplies.

We cannot fight Ebola in isolation. People need functioning health services, clean water, sanitation, food, protection, and livelihoods. Above all, they need trust.

Excellencies,

The people delivering this response are taking extraordinary risks.

More than 40 health workers have died from Ebola while working to save others. Treatment centres and ambulances have been attacked.

These front-line responders must be protected.

Preparedness efforts have increased in neighboring countries, particularly South Sudan and the Central African Republic, both already confronting severe humanitarian emergencies.

Last week, WHO declared Uganda free of this outbreak after 42 days with no reported Ebola cases.

Excellencies,

The revised 2026 DRC Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan calls for $2.1 billion, including $300 million for Ebola-related activities across the humanitarian family.

More than $1 billion has been secured, but half of the funding gap remains. The virus is not waiting for us to find it.

Through the Central Emergency Response Fund, with thanks to our generous donors to that fund, I have allocated over $57 million for response and preparedness in the DRC and neighboring countries. And of course, country-based and regional pooled funding is also stepping up.

To close, Excellencies,

Last week, the Secretary-General called out the indifference surrounding this crisis. He is right to do so.

An outbreak spreading at this speed should command the world’s attention.

The DRC is doing its part – the international community must do ours.

So, my appeals are straightforward.

First, use your influence collectively and individually to keep this crisis where it should be on the international agenda. Do not wait for Ebola to cross borders before you act.

Secondly, we need access. Humanitarian personnel and supplies must move safely and swiftly into and within the DRC. We need borders kept open. We need obstacles to the response removed.

And thirdly, the funding. We need increased, flexible support for the Ebola response and the wider humanitarian operation.

Time is not on our side.

We have the experience, the tools, extraordinary people risking their lives to stop this epidemic.

What we need now is political will, access, and resources.

We have beaten Ebola before. And we can do it again.

Thank you, excellencies.

fields.title: Afrique de l’Ouest et centrale : Derniers événements en bref (du 25 au 31 août 2026)
fields.body:
**République démocratique du Congo**  
*La réponse à Ebola s’étend à mesure que l’épidémie se propage*

OCHA signale que les partenaires humanitaires et sanitaires renforcent la riposte contre Ébola en République démocratique du Congo, en déployant plus de 2 500 volontaires et personnels de la protection civile au cours des prochains mois. Les partenaires ajoutent 35 équipes mobiles et 286 équipes communautaires à travers l'Ituri, le Nord-Kivu et la Tshopo, tout en étendant leurs opérations au Haut-Uélé et au Bas-Uélé. Ces équipes soutiendront la surveillance, l'engagement communautaire, l'assistance psychosociale, ainsi que des enterrements sûrs et dignes afin d'aider à prévenir toute transmission supplémentaire.

L'OMS indique que 60 pour cent des décès surviennent dans les communautés, ce qui souligne la nécessité d'accroître les capacités d'inhumation. Au 30 août, les autorités sanitaires nationales avaient signalé 6 100 cas confirmés d'Ébola et 2 950 décès, avec un taux de létalité de 48 pour cent. La couverture de la recherche des contacts reste supérieure à l'objectif opérationnel de 85 pour cent dans les zones touchées.

**Tchad**  
 La situation épidémique du choléra semble s'améliorer

Les rapports font état de signes d'amélioration de l'épidémie de choléra au Tchad, avec une baisse des cas quotidiens et aucun nouveau décès signalé depuis le 23 août. Au 25 août, 332 cas et 14 décès avaient été enregistrés dans cinq districts touchés, soit un taux de létalité de 4,2 pour cent. Les activités de vaccination et d'intervention rapide sont intensifiées, notamment dans les nouveaux foyers épidémiques.

Toutefois, les contraintes d'accès, les graves lacunes en matière d'eau, d'assainissement et d'hygiène, ainsi que la surpopulation dans les sites de déplacés continuent d'entraver la riposte et d'accroître le risque de reprise de la transmission.

**Nigéria**  
*La transmission du choléra recule dans l'État de Borno grâce à une intervention renforcée*

La transmission du choléra et les décès diminuent dans l'État de Borno à la suite de quatre mois d'interventions coordonnées en matière de santé, d'eau, d'assainissement et d'hygiène, soutenues par 4 millions de dollars américains du CERF et par un financement additionnel du Fonds humanitaire pour le Nigéria. Au 24 août, 59 035 cas suspects et 314 décès avaient été signalés dans 22 zones de gouvernement local depuis le mois de mai, Monguno restant un foyer épidémique. Plus de 55 000 patients se sont rétablis.

Les autorités gouvernementales et les partenaires ont renforcé la surveillance et la prise en charge des cas, en déployant 78 équipes d'intervention rapide et en soutenant 91 centres de traitement et de réhydratation orale dotés de 961 lits. Les campagnes de vaccination ont touché environ 2,8 millions de personnes à Maiduguri et à Jere. Les partenaires ont également chloré 411 points d'eau, améliorant ainsi l'accès à l'eau potable pour plus de 862 000 personnes.

**République centrafricaine**  
*Les déplacements transfrontaliers renforcent les craintes liées au virus Ebola*

Les mouvements transfrontaliers entre la République centrafricaine et la République démocratique du Congo suscitent des inquiétudes quant à une propagation potentielle d'Ébola. Au 24 août, cinq villages proches de la frontière restaient abandonnés, des civils ayant apparemment fui vers Zapaï en RDC, près de la province du Bas-Uélé touchée par la maladie.

Les autorités gouvernementales et les partenaires humanitaires renforcent la surveillance, les capacités d'isolement, les points de contrôle et la sensibilisation des communautés. Le CERF a alloué 3 millions de dollars américains pour soutenir les efforts de préparation et de prévention contre Ébola dans la région. Aucun cas d'Ébola n'a été confirmé en République centrafricaine à ce jour.

fields.title: West and Central Africa: Latest Events at a glance (25–31 August 2026)
fields.body:
**Democratic Republic of the Congo**  
*Ebola response expands as outbreak spreads*

OCHA reports that humanitarian and health partners are scaling up the Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, deploying more than 2,500 volunteers and civil protection personnel over the coming months. Partners are adding 35 mobile teams and 286 community-based teams across Ituri, North Kivu, and Tshopo, while extending operations to Haut-Uélé and Bas-Uélé. The teams will support surveillance, community engagement, psychosocial assistance, and safe and dignified burials to help prevent further transmission.

The World Health Organization reports that 60 per cent of deaths are occurring in communities, highlighting the need for increased burial capacity. As of 30 August, national health authorities had reported 6,100 confirmed Ebola cases and 2,950 deaths, with a case fatality ratio of 48 per cent. Contact tracing coverage remains above the operational target of 85 per cent in affected areas.

**Chad**  
*Cholera transmission shows signs of improvement*

Reports highlight signs of improvement in Chad’s cholera outbreak, with daily cases falling and no new deaths reported since 23 August. As of 25 August, 332 cases and 14 deaths had been recorded across five affected districts, representing a case fatality ratio of 4.2 per cent. Vaccination and rapid-response activities are being scaled up, including in emerging hotspots. However, access constraints, severe water, sanitation and hygiene gaps, and overcrowding in displacement sites continue to hamper the response and raise the risk of renewed transmission.

**Nigeria**  
*Cholera transmission declines in Borno State following scaled-up response*

Cholera transmission and fatalities are declining in Borno State following four months of coordinated health and water, sanitation and hygiene interventions, supported by US$4 million from the CERF and additional Nigeria Humanitarian Fund funding. As of 24 August, 59,035 suspected cases and 314 deaths had been reported across 22 local government areas since May, with Monguno remaining a hotspot. More than 55,000 patients have recovered.

Government authorities and partners have strengthened surveillance and case management, deploying 78 rapid-response teams and supporting 91 treatment and oral rehydration facilities with 961 beds. Vaccination campaigns have reached about 2.8 million people in Maiduguri and Jere. Partners have also chlorinated 411 water points, improving access to safe water for more than 862,000 people.

**Central African Republic**  
*Cross-border movements heighten Ebola concerns*

Cross-border movements between the Central African Republic and the Democratic Republic of the Congo are raising concerns over the potential spread of Ebola. As of 24 August, five villages near the border remained abandoned, with civilians reportedly fleeing to Zapaï in the DR Congo, close to Ebola-affected Bas-Uélé province.

Government authorities and humanitarian partners are strengthening surveillance, isolation capacity, checkpoints and community awareness. CERF has allocated US$3 million to support Ebola preparedness and prevention efforts in the area. No Ebola cases have been confirmed in the Central African Republic to date.

fields.title: Treatment and prevention research on Bundibugyo virus disease must deliver for children, not leave them behind
fields.body:
*MSF calls on researchers, donors and manufacturers to take urgent actions*

**London, September 1, 2026**

**Background:**

[**In a commentary published in** ***The Lancet*** **today**](https://share.google/bFZFbzsLhTbCTPlub), MSF calls for urgent action from all stakeholders involved in research on Bundibugyo virus treatment and prevention to ensure that children are meaningfully included in planned, evidence-generating research on medical countermeasures, and, in particular, have timely access to paediatric formulations for ongoing trials of oral post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).

The current Ebola disease outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has disproportionately affected children. As of [**4 August 2026 and among confirmed cases for whom age is reported,**](https://insp.cd/sitrep-n082-mve-b_04-08-2026/) the proportion of children under five years old who were diagnosed and who subsequently died from Bundibugyo virus disease was significantly higher than that of adults.

Delayed inclusion in trials, lack of paediatric dosing guidance, and safety concerns are familiar barriers to access to medical countermeasures for children and pregnant and breastfeeding women and girls (PBWG.) Currently, the [**EBO-PEP study, which began on 14 July 2026**](https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20260714-who-launches-first-trial-of-antiviral-to-prevent-bundibugyo-strain-of-ebola), is evaluating the oral antiviral obeldesivir for preventing infection following high-risk exposure to Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus. If this proves to be effective, it could offer a practical and scalable method to protect people who have had recent contact with a case of Ebola. While children weighing less than 30 kg (approximately 12 years old or younger) are excluded from the trial in its original design, we can expect that a planned protocol amendment to include children over 20kg will soon be accepted. ​ However, owing to the lack of an available paediatric formulation of obeldesivir and the absence of published data supporting tablet crushing or dissolution, children under 20 kg (6 years old or under) are still excluded from this study. While the trial is conducting a sub-protocol for those excluded consisting of intravenous (IV) remdesivir, a daily IV treatment course over 10 days is operationally very difficult in outbreak settings, especially for young children. Gilead has recently expressed willingness to make paediatric formulations of obeldesivir available soon. It is yet to be seen when the trial with oral formulations will start. ​

**Dr Neal Russell, Paediatric Advisor, MSF:** ​

“Too often, the inclusion of children in the development of medical countermeasures to address public health emergencies is left to the ‘small print’ but today, with children at a disproportionately high risk of dying if infected with Ebola in the current outbreak in DRC, their inclusion is paramount.

"Researchers, donors and other stakeholders must urgently support a paediatric obeldesivir sub-study, build on existing dosing guidance, and accelerate the evaluation of other oral antivirals and monoclonal antibodies as post-exposure prophylaxis. We need to generate the evidence now so that children can access effective preventive treatments alongside everyone else, not after the outbreak is over.

"Gilead – the pharmaceutical corporation manufacturing obeldesivir – has committed to reproduce the antiviral in its paediatric formulation. We hope that Gilead will provide a clear and accelerated timeline for doing so, and that stakeholders can organise paediatric studies with this formulation, or with modified adult tablets as soon as possible, so that all children at risk can be included in studies evaluating which post-exposure prophylaxis options are most practical, timely and effective. ”

For more information, please contact:

fields.title: Cluster Protection RDC : Points saillants de la situation de protection en République démocratique du Congo du mois de juillet 2026
fields.body:
Au cours du mois de juillet 2026, la situation de protection en République démocratique du Congo s’est davantage détériorée, dans un contexte marqué par la multiplication des confrontations armées, l’expansion de l’épidémie d’Ebola Bundibugyo et la persistance des contraintes d’accès humanitaire.

Les provinces de l’Est, particulièrement le Nord-Kivu, l’Ituri et le Sud-Kivu, ont concentré les incidents les plus graves, entraînant d’importants déplacements de population et une aggravation de la vulnérabilité des communautés affectées. Le Tanganyika a également été touché par l’activisme des groupes armés, les conflits communautaires, les incendies, la criminalité et les mouvements de population.

Dans plusieurs zones, les civils ont été directement touchés par les affrontements, les bombardements, les tirs d’obus, les enlèvements, les violences sexuelles, les pillages et, dans certains contextes, l’utilisation de drones, entraînant des pertes en vies humaines, des dommages aux infrastructures sanitaires et éducatives ainsi que des déplacements massifs.

Parallèlement, la progression de l’épidémie d’Ebola a accentué les risques de protection, notamment pour les personnes déplacées, en limitant l’accès aux soins et en alimentant les tensions sociales.

Les femmes, les enfants, les personnes déplacées internes et les retournés demeurent les groupes les plus exposés aux violations et aux risques de protection à travers le pays.

fields.title: République Centrafricaine: Analyse de Protection - Mise à jour de la situation de protection (Juillet 2026)
fields.body:
En 2026, la situation de protection de la population en République centrafricaine demeure préoccupante et complexe. Les affrontements et conflits impliquant les hommes en armes ont fait de nombreuses victimes parmi lesquelles, les personnes déplacées internes dont la vulnérabilité s’est accentuée du fait de nouveaux déplacements et des violences subies.

A ce jour, 428 227 personnes restent encore déplacées dans le pays du fait des violences persistantes entre les Forces armées Centrafricaines \[FACA\] seuls ou conjointement avec les Autres Personnels de Sécurité \[APS\] et les groupes armés, mais aussi des tensions intercommunautaires. Les risques majeurs de protection persistent et sont aggravés par la réduction progressive, depuis 2025, des capacités et de la présence des organisations et interventions de protection.

Les sites de déplacement et les communautés hôtes d’accueil sont surchargés, ce qui accentue les vulnérabilités, notamment pour les femmes, les enfants les personnes en situation de handicap et les personnes âgées. Le retrait progressif de certaines localités entamé par la MINUSCA réduit déjà les moyens de protection des civils. Par ailleurs, l’accès humanitaire reste limité dans certaines zones en raison de l’insécurité et des contraintes physiques et logistiques, ce qui entrave la mise en oeuvre efficace des activités et des réponses de protection. Les mécanismes communautaires de protection restent affaiblis, tandis que les capacités institutionnelles nationales restent limitées pour assurer une réponse durable. Ces défis combinés maintiennent un environnement d’insécurité prolongée, compliquant la protection des PDI et la recherche de solutions durables à leurs besoins.

Au cours de la période couverte par cette analyse le Cluster Protection a identifié les risques de protection prioritaires suivant, nécessitant une attention immédiate :

1\. Violences basées sur le genre et violences liées aux conflits  
2\. Attaques contre les civils et les biens civils  
3\. Recrutement forcé et association d'enfants avec des groupes armés  
4\. Restrictions à la liberté de mouvement et déplacements forcés  
5\. Présence de mines et d'engins explosifs

fields.title: DRC: Ebola response must step up as millions of children return to school | The IRC
fields.body:
**IRC works with teachers, parents, and communities to keep Ebola out of classrooms**

Bunia, Democratic Republic of Congo, August 31, 2026 — As millions of children across the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) return to school this week, the close contact typical of classrooms and communal dormitories could present new challenges for Ebola containment efforts already underway. The International Rescue Committee (IRC) is working to keep students safe, reduce transmission risk, and strengthen trust and prevention efforts as schools reopen.

With the outbreak in its fourth month, Ebola case numbers continue to climb across eastern DRC, and health authorities have recorded more than 5,945 cases and over 2,862 deaths. Already by early August, [743 of those cases and 330 of those deaths were children](https://www.unicef.org/press-releases/dr-congo-ebola-child-deaths-pass-300-unicef-warns-outbreak-also-threatens-essential). In higher-risk areas, including the epicenter Bunia, schools await guidance from health authorities, while in lower-risk areas, schools open on September 1st. The IRC is redoubling its prevention efforts across 30 schools in Ituri, training teachers on Ebola prevention and child protection, running age-appropriate awareness sessions for children, and working with school authorities, parents and communities to make the return to school safer, in line with health authorities guidance.

"Children are among the most vulnerable to this outbreak. Almost one in three deaths is a child, and far too many children have lost one or both parents and family members,” said Hannah Gibbin, Ebola response team lead for the IRC in Bunia. “Children have the right to learn safely, even in the middle of an Ebola outbreak. Education gives back what this outbreak has taken away from them: stability, connection, and a sense of normal life. This is what we are trying to protect, working with school authorities, teachers, families, communities and authorities to reinforce Ebola awareness and prevention. Education cannot be the next casualty of this outbreak."

The IRC has been responding to Ebola outbreaks in this region since 2014: our efforts draw on those lessons and are tailored to each local context and impacted communities. The IRC is working deep within the community to combat misinformation and deliver emergency supplies and hygiene services to reinforce prevention. The IRC also addresses the psychosocial impacts of the outbreak, training health personnel and community leaders in mental health and psychosocial support. This work is crucial for children as they face family separation, stigma, psychosocial distress, and neglect that impact them in profound ways. The IRC identifies and refers children who need support, provides psychosocial support, sets up safe referral pathways, and works to counter stigma through community messages.

As children return to classrooms, teachers, parents and communities are the first ones able to protect them from Ebola, support their wellbeing, and ensure continuity of learning. But they cannot do this alone. More support and funding are urgently needed to help schools strengthen prevention and hygiene measures, provide psychosocial support and ensure teachers have the tools and help they need to respond to children’s needs. Investing in these measures is essential not only to protect children from Ebola, but to ensure that schools remain safe, supportive places where children can learn, play and thrive.

fields.title: UNICEF Humanitarian Situation Report No. 1 (BVD Outbreak in DRC: Regional Preparedness and Readiness in Neighboring and At-Risk Countries), July 2026
fields.body:
**Highlights**

- Regional preparedness efforts continue across at-risk countries as the Bundibugyo Virus Disease (BVD) outbreak remains active in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Uganda officially declared the end of its outbreak on 28 July 2026, and no confirmed cases have been reported in other neighboring countries to date. Nevertheless, sustained population movements, porous borders and humanitarian vulnerabilities continue to present a risk of cross-border transmission, requiring heightened vigilance and preparedness measures.
- UNICEF is supporting governments in 10 priority at-risk countries to strengthen readiness, early detection and response capacity. Efforts focus on infection prevention and control (IPC), WASH, risk communication and community engagement (RCCE), surveillance, emergency coordination and preparedness at key points of entry. Countries continue to conduct simulation exercises, train frontline workers, engage communities and pre-position essential supplies to ensure rapid detection and containment of any imported case.
- Cross-border preparedness remains a key regional priority. UNICEF is supporting coordination among neighboring countries, including through regular preparedness reviews, information sharing and technical support to strengthen operational readiness and ensure a harmonized regional approach to outbreak prevention and response.
- Funding gaps continue to constrain preparedness activities across the region. UNICEF requires US$25.4 million to sustain preparedness and readiness efforts in 10 at-risk countries. Timely and predictable financing remains essential to maintain readiness capacities and address vulnerabilities before international spread occurs.

fields.title: UNICEF Cameroon Cholera Outbreak Flash Update No. 3, 23 July-24 August 2026
fields.body:
**Situation Update**

• During epidemiological week 34, two additional health districts, Maroua II and Mokolo, reported laboratory-confirmed cholera cases, bringing the total number of confirmed affected districts to 10: Mada, Makary, Kousseri, Fotokol, Kolofata, Mora, Maroua I, Maroua II, Maroua III and Mokolo. In addition, Mozogo and Gazawa health districts remain under suspected cholera status. This expansion reflects the continued geographic spread of cholera across the Far North Region and underscores the need for sustained surveillance and response efforts in affected and at-risk areas.

• Children and adolescents remain particularly at risk, with a median age of 12 years among reported cases. The age of affected individuals ranges from 3 months to 87 years, highlighting that the outbreak is affecting all age groups, while placing a significant burden on children.

• UNICEF continues to support the government-led response across key sectors, including Health, Water, Hygiene, and Sanitation (WASH), Social and Behavior Change (SBC), Accountability to Affected Population, Child Protection, Youth participation, Nutrition and overall response coordination.

fields.title: Tchad - Mise à jour sur la sécurité alimentaire : Les déficits pluviométriques aggravent l’insécurité alimentaire dans l’Est du Tchad, Août 2026 - Janvier 2027
fields.body:
**Messages clé**

- **Les résultats de Crise ! (Phase 3 ! de l’IPC) et de Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC) se maintiendront entre août 2026 et janvier 2027 dans les provinces d’Ouaddaï, Sila, Wadi Fira et Ennedi Est.** Les réfugiés continuent d’arriver, dépendant largement du marché et de l’assistance alimentaire. Leurs pressions sur les moyens d’existence de la population hôte augmente à un moment où les conditions de soudures très sévères, occasionnant d’importants déficits de consommation alimentaire. Une amélioration chez les populations hôtes reste cependant attendue avec les récoltes en octobre.
- **Des résultats de Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC) sont attendus dans la province du Lac jusqu’en janvier 2027.** Les conditions sécuritaires se dégradent et la saison accuse un retard pendant que les attaques des groupes armés terroristes persistent. La dégradation des moyens d’existence, notamment la pêche et l’élevage, entraîne une baisse des revenus. Des déficits de consommation alimentaire sont observés chez les déplacés internes et les populations hôtes. Toutefois, une amélioration vers des résultats de Stress (Phase 2 de l’IPC) est attendue entre octobre et janvier 2027 dans le département de Wayi avec l’arrivée des récoltes.
- **Des résultats de Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC) sont anticipés entre août et septembre 2026 dans le Kanem et le nord Barh-El-Gazel.** Dans cette zone pastorale, la saison a accusé un retard jusqu’en août. Les ménages, dépendants des marchés, restent confrontés à des coûts élevés d’entretien du bétail, et à la détérioration de la plupart de leurs sources de revenus. Le faible pouvoir d’achat les pousse à effectuer des ventes atypiques de leur capital productif. À partir d’octobre, ces conditions s’amélioreront ainsi que la consommation alimentaire des ménages.
- **Un retard d’installation de la saison, avec des précipitations inférieures à la moyenne, est observé dans plusieurs régions du pays.** Une soudure très difficile est en cours dans plusieurs localités. La quasi-totalité des ménages dépend fortement du marché, alors que le retard empêche la restauration des revenus agricoles typiques qui devraient faciliter l’accès aux aliments.

*Ce rapport fournit une mise à jour des* [*perspectives sur la sécurité alimentaire de juin 2026 à janvier 2027*](https://fews.net/fr/west-africa/tchad/perspectives-sur-la-securite-alimentaire/juin-2026) *et des* [*messages clés de juillet 2026*](https://fews.net/fr/west-africa/tchad/mise-jour-des-messages-cles/juillet-2026)*. L’analyse est basée sur les informations disponibles au 16 août 2026.*

fields.title: République centrafricaine - Mise à jour sur la sécurité alimentaire : Les résultats de Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC) persistent dans les zones enclavés et affectées par l’insécurité, Août 2026 - Janvier 2027
fields.body:
**Messages clé**

- **Entre août 2026 et janvier 2027, des résultats de Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC) devraient persister dans les préfectures les plus affectées par l’insécurité et l’enclavement, notamment dans le nord-est, le nord-ouest et le Haut-Mbomou.** Dans ces zones, l’insécurité persistante continuera de limiter l’accès aux champs, aux opportunités de revenus et aux principaux axes commerciaux. Malgré les récoltes attendues à partir d’octobre dans le nord, les productions resteront inférieures à la moyenne dans plusieurs localités affectées par les conflits et les déplacements de population. Les ménages continueront de recourir à l’endettement et à la vente d’actifs, toutefois, ils seront tout de même confrontés à des déficits de consommation alimentaire, réduisant la fréquence et la quantité de leurs repas.
- **Les conditions de marché demeurent dégradées dans plusieurs zones du pays en raison des perturbations persistantes de l’approvisionnement et de la pénurie de carburant observée depuis juillet.** Les difficultés de réapprovisionnement en carburant, combinées à la dégradation saisonnière des routes et aux contraintes sécuritaires, continuent de renchérir les coûts de transport et de commercialisation.
- **À partir d’octobre, des résultats de Stress (Phase 2 de l’IPC) devraient prédominer jusqu’en janvier 2027 dans la Ouaka, le Mbomou, la Basse-Kotto, la Nana-Mambéré, ainsi que dans les préfectures du centre et du sud-ouest.** L’arrivée des récoltes de maïs, d’arachide, de manioc et de riz permettra une amélioration progressive de la disponibilité alimentaire, la reconstitution des stocks et une réduction de la dépendance aux marchés. Toutefois, les prix alimentaires supérieurs à la moyenne, les coûts de transport élevés et les revenus encore limités continueront d’empêcher de nombreux ménages pauvres de couvrir pleinement leurs dépenses essentielles non alimentaires.

*Ce rapport fournit une mise à jour des*[ *perspectives sur la sécurité alimentaire pour le juin 2026* ](https://fews.net/fr/west-africa/republique-centrafricaine/perspectives-sur-la-securite-alimentaire/juin-2026)*et des* [*messages clés de juillet 2027*](https://fews.net/fr/west-africa/republique-centrafricaine/mise-jour-des-messages-cles/juillet-2026)*. L’analyse est basée sur les informations disponibles au 25 août 2026.*

fields.title: République démocratique du Congo - Mise à jour sur la sécurité alimentaire : La poursuite des violences présage une soudure précoce pour les ménages, Août 2026 - Janvier 2027
fields.body:
**Messages clé**

- **Les résultats de Crise (Phase 3 de l'IPC) devraient persister jusqu'en janvier 2027 à l’est du pays.** Les conflits continueront de perturber les moyens d’existence, les marchés et les commerces. Ces perturbations devraient accroître les déficits de consommation et le recours des ménages aux stratégies d’adaptation négatives, telles que l’endettement et la vente d’actifs productifs, et entrainer une soudure précoce à partir de septembre. Les ménages les plus touchés par les conflits, ceux situés à proximité des lignes de front où la mobilité est fortement restreinte, devraient faire face à des résultats d'Urgence (Phase 4 de l'IPC). A partir de mi-décembre, les ménages ayant pu cultiver durant la saison agricole 2 (S2) devraient voir leur sécurité alimentaire s'améliorer, mais une proportion importante des ménages pauvres restera en Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC).
- **Des résultats de Stress (Phase 2 de l'IPC) devraient persister jusqu’en janvier dans la majeure partie du pays.** La baisse de pouvoir d’achat et les moyens d’existence dégradés continueront d’entrainer une consommation alimentaire minimale adéquate, mais les ménages ne pourront pas couvrir leurs besoins essentiels non alimentaires. Certains territoires aux Kasaïs, impactés par les conflits communautaires, les déplacements répétés et les pertes d’actifs, seront en Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC) durant la période de soudure.
- **L’épidémie de la maladie à virus Ebola poursuit son expansion géographique et en nombre de cas**. Les mesures imposées pour la lutte contre la propagation de cette maladie, notamment les fermetures de frontières et les barrières routières, réduisent les flux transfrontaliers par endroit et la circulation des personnes, fragilisant les systèmes d’échanges. L’épidémie perturbe l’approvisionnement des produits alimentaires, tout en entraînant une perte de revenus pour des milliers de ménages pauvres vivant d’activités transfrontalières. À l’approche de la soudure, la disponibilité alimentaire devrait commencer à se dégrader, entraînant une dépendance accrue aux marchés.

*Ce rapport fournit une mise à jour des* [*perspectives sur la sécurité alimentaire de juin 2026 à janvier 2027*](https://fews.net/fr/southern-africa/republique-democratique-du-congo/perspectives-sur-la-securite-alimentaire/juin-2026) *et des* [*messages clés de juillet 2026.*](https://fews.net/fr/southern-africa/republique-democratique-du-congo/mise-jour-des-messages-cles/juillet-2026/print) *L’analyse est basée sur les informations disponibles au 25 août 2026.*

fields.title: Cameroun - Mise à jour des messages clés : Des récoltes inférieures à la moyenne n’apportent qu’un répit temporaire, tandis que les déficits liés au conflit maintiennent Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC), Juillet 2026 - Janvier 2027
fields.body:
**Messages clé**

- **Les départements de Mayo-Sava, Mayo-Tsanaga et Logone-et-Chari, dans l’Extrême-Nord, affectés par le conflit, devraient rester en Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC) pendant le reste de la période de soudure de juin à août,** les ménages pauvres étant confrontés à des déficits de consommation alimentaire dans un contexte de faible pouvoir d’achat, de forte dépendance aux marchés et de prix alimentaires élevés. Les récoltes de septembre à novembre devraient améliorer la disponibilité et l’accès aux aliments, permettant une consommation alimentaire minimalement adéquate et une amélioration vers les résultats de Stress (Phase 2 de l’IPC) au niveau de la zone jusqu’en janvier 2027. Toutefois, les déficits de production liés au conflit continueront de limiter les revenus issus de la vente des récoltes et les possibilités de travail, réduisant ainsi la capacité des ménages à satisfaire leurs besoins essentiels non alimentaires. Par conséquent, une faible proportion des ménages — en particulier les très pauvres — devrait rester en Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC) ou pire jusqu’en janvier 2027.
- **Les résultats se sont améliorés, passant de Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC) à Stress (Phase 2 de l’IPC) dans certaines parties du Nord-Ouest et du Sud-Ouest** à la suite des récoltes de juillet, grâce à l’amélioration de la disponibilité et de l’accès aux aliments. Toutefois, les récoltes inférieures à la moyenne limitent les stocks alimentaires des ménages, ainsi que les revenus tirés de la vente des récoltes et de la main-d'œuvre agricole, empêchant de nombreux ménages de couvrir leurs dépenses essentielles non alimentaires. À partir de novembre, l’épuisement précoce de ces stocks entraînera une dépendance accrue aux marchés ; conjuguée à des revenus limités et à la hausse des prix alimentaires, le pouvoir d’achat sera encore affaibli et l’adoption de stratégies d’adaptation négatives sévères sera favorisée — notamment la vente d’actifs et le renoncement aux dépenses de santé. Cette situation entraînera un retour généralisé à des résultats de Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC) jusqu’en janvier 2027. Une situation de Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC) devrait également persister au niveau de la zone de juillet 2026 à janvier 2027 dans les les divisions les plus reculées et dangereuses de Bui, Momo, Menchum, Lebialem et Ndian, où les ménages sont confrontés à d’importants déficits de récolte et à des pertes de moyens d’existence.
- **Des résultats de Stress (Phase 2 de l’IPC) devraient persister jusqu’en janvier 2027 dans le Mbéré (Adamaoua), la Kadey et le Lom-et-Djérem (Est), ainsi qu’à Yaoundé et Douala.** Bien que les récoltes de juillet à septembre aient amélioré la disponibilité alimentaire et contribuent à atténuer certains prix alimentaires, les ménages resteront dans l’incapacité de satisfaire leurs besoins essentiels non alimentaires. Dans l’Est et l’Adamaoua, la pression persistante exercée par les réfugiés de la République centrafricaine sur les prix alimentaires et les moyens d’existence restera la principale contrainte. Dans les centres urbains de Yaoundé et Douala, fortement dépendants des marchés, la forte concurrence pour les possibilités limitées de travail occasionnel — exacerbée par la présence de populations déplacées — continuera de limiter les revenus dans un contexte de prix alimentaires durablement élevés. Les ménages très pauvres, y compris les réfugiés, resteront en Crise (Phase 3 de l’IPC) pendant toute la période de projection.
- **Les perspectives de production agricole restent inférieures à la moyenne dans les zones de la partie nord du pays affectées par le conflit, malgré des précipitations généralement favorables en juillet,** qui ont favorisé une croissance normale des cultures et amélioré les conditions des pâturages dans une grande partie de la région. Dans ces zones, l’insécurité persistante et les perturbations des activités agricoles continuent de limiter la participation des ménages aux activités de production. La hausse des prix des engrais — qui étaient de 30 à 40 pour cent plus élevés en juillet qu’en mars —, conjuguée à la réduction de l’assistance humanitaire et à l’accès limité aux intrants subventionnés par le gouvernement, a encore restreint l’accès des ménages pauvres aux intrants pendant la période critique d’application des engrais de juin à août.
